title: Alerting Done Right
description: Learn symptom-based alerting, fight alert fatigue, build runbook-linked alerts, and design on-call rotations that don't burn people out.

segments.text: I've seen teams with four thousand active alerts. Engineers get paged two hundred times per week. They start ignoring alerts, muting channels, and the one critical alert that signals a real outage gets buried under noise. Alert fatigue kills reliability faster than any technical failure.

There are two types of alerts. Symptom-based: users are experiencing high latency. Cause-based: CPU is at ninety percent. Always alert on symptoms, not causes. High CPU doesn't necessarily mean users are affected. High latency always means users are affected. Causes help you diagnose, but symptoms tell you to act.

A good alert has three properties. It's actionable — someone can do something about it right now. It's urgent — it needs attention within minutes, not days. And it's real — it fires less than five percent false positive rate. If any of these fail, the alert shouldn't page someone at 3 AM.

The best alerting strategy uses error budget burn rates from the previous lesson. Instead of alerting on error rate greater than one percent, alert when your error budget burn rate exceeds fourteen times normal for the last hour. This accounts for baseline noise and only fires when you're genuinely burning through your budget.
Your team gets paged one hundred and fifty times per month. Sixty percent are false positives. Morale is cratering. What's your systematic approach to fixing this?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you reduce 150 monthly pages with 60% false positive rate to a manageable level?

segments.text: Every alert must link to a runbook. The on-call engineer getting paged at 3 AM shouldn't need to reverse-engineer what the alert means. The runbook answers: what does this alert mean, what's the impact, what are the diagnostic steps, what's the mitigation, and who to escalate to. Google mandates runbooks for every production alert.

PagerDuty escalation policies prevent single points of failure. Primary on-call has five minutes to acknowledge. If not, escalate to secondary. After fifteen minutes, escalate to the engineering manager. For SEV-1 incidents, create a bridge call automatically. The goal is ensuring every critical alert gets human attention.

On-call rotations that work: weekly rotations with a maximum of one in six ratio — each engineer is on call at most one week out of six. Compensate with time off or extra pay. Follow-the-sun across time zones so nobody gets paged at night. Uber moved to regional on-call and reduced after-hours pages by seventy percent.

Run a monthly alert review. For each alert that fired, ask: was it actionable? Did someone need to do something? If an alert consistently fires without action, delete it. At LinkedIn, they cut alerts by sixty percent through quarterly reviews without missing a single real incident.
You're designing an alerting strategy for a payment service with a ninety-nine point nine nine percent SLO. What alerts would you create, and what would your escalation policy look like?
segments.thought_prompt: Design alerting for a payment service at 99.99% SLO. What fires a page vs a ticket vs nothing?

segments.text: Great alerting is about signal over noise. Alert on symptoms not causes, link every alert to a runbook, use burn rate instead of threshold alerts, review and prune alerts monthly, and design on-call rotations that respect human limits. The best alert system is one where every page means a real problem that needs a human right now.
